california-dmv-road-signs-practice.heading: California: choose a curb for the stop you need
california-dmv-road-signs-practice.intro: Read beyond the paint. Decide what you are doing, how long you need, and whether you are allowed in the space. These original cases are separate from the scored curb checkpoint.

examples.title: A passenger pickup turns into a wait
examples.question: You reach a white curb in California for a passenger pickup. The passenger texts that they will be out in ten minutes. Can you wait where you are if you stay behind the wheel?
steps: No. The white curb is for the brief stop needed to pick up or drop off a passenger, not for waiting for someone to arrive.
Move to a legal waiting spot instead of treating the white curb as short-term parking.
When your passenger is ready, return to an available pickup space and leave after they get in.
examples.mistake: Staying in the driver's seat does not turn waiting into loading a passenger.
examples.check: You find an open green curb marked 15 MIN PARKING. The restriction is in force, and no other sign limits you. Can you use it for the ten-minute wait?
examples.answer: Yes. It allows time-limited parking. Stay within the posted 15 minutes; if the pickup takes longer, leave or find another legal spot.

source.label: California Driver's Handbook: Parking at Colored Curbs

examples.title: A parking space and its access aisle are different
examples.question: You are driving a passenger with their valid disabled-person placard. The marked accessible space is open, and a striped access aisle is beside it. Where may you park?
steps: Use the marked accessible parking space when driving the eligible passenger and displaying their valid placard.
Keep the striped access aisle clear. It is space for people and wheelchair lifts, not an extra parking spot.
Check the whole vehicle fits inside the parking space. Briefly stopping across the stripes to unload still blocks the access area.
examples.mistake: A placard gives parking privileges in the marked space; it does not make the adjacent stripes part of that space.
examples.check: The next day you drive back alone for your own errand and still have the passenger's placard. May you use the accessible space?
examples.answer: No. The placard is not yours to use for your own trip. Park in a space you are allowed to use without it.

source.label: California DMV: Disabled Person Parking Placards and Plates

illinois-dmv-road-signs-practice.heading: Illinois: when does the work-zone speed limit apply?
illinois-dmv-road-signs-practice.intro: The school-zone cases ask you to check the time and whether children are near traffic. Do not carry those conditions over to a posted Illinois work-zone limit. These original cases do not affect the image quiz score.

examples.title: The crew is gone, but the limit stays
examples.question: At 9 p.m. on a normally 55 mph Illinois road, you pass a WORK ZONE SPEED LIMIT 45 sign. Cones still narrow the lane, but you see no workers. Which maximum applies in the signed zone?
steps: The posted work-zone maximum is 45 mph. The usual 55 mph limit does not apply in that signed zone.
The sign is still in force at night, even without workers present.
Treat 45 mph as a maximum, not a target. Slow further if the narrowed lane, traffic or visibility requires it.
examples.mistake: Do not look for a crew to decide whether a posted work-zone limit counts. The school-zone time and presence conditions are a different rule.
examples.check: The same 45 mph sign remains in force, but heavy rain cuts visibility. Are you supposed to hold 45 mph?
examples.answer: No. 45 mph still caps your speed, but slow below it as needed for the rain and limited visibility.

source.label: Illinois Rules of the Road 2026: Construction Zones, page 25

examples.title: A warning is not a new speed limit
examples.question: You see an orange ROAD WORK AHEAD sign in Illinois. The last posted limit was 55 mph. You have not yet passed a new speed-limit sign, and the lane is narrowing. Does the orange sign by itself set a 45 mph limit?
steps: No. ROAD WORK AHEAD warns of a change ahead. It does not set a numerical limit.
Slow for the narrowing lane and watch for traffic control. Do not assume that driving at the last posted maximum is safe.
Look for a regulatory speed-limit sign. Read the posted number instead of guessing a work-zone speed.
examples.mistake: Orange tells you to expect temporary conditions. It does not tell you how many miles per hour to subtract.
examples.check: A little farther on you pass a WORK ZONE SPEED LIMIT 40 sign. You still see no workers. What changes?
examples.answer: 40 mph is now the posted maximum in the signed zone even without workers. Go slower if the conditions require it.

source.label: Illinois DOT Traffic Control Devices: Speed Limit Signs and Warning Signs, sections 39-2.08 and 39-2.09

pennsylvania-dmv-road-signs-practice.heading: Pennsylvania: when two one-way streets meet at a red light
pennsylvania-dmv-road-signs-practice.intro: Practice deciding when a turn is permitted, not just reading the arrow on a sign. These examples use a steady circular red light and do not affect your quiz score.

examples.title: One-way street to one-way street
examples.question: You are in the left lane of a one-way street in Pennsylvania, facing a round red light. The crossing street is one-way to your left and no sign forbids the turn. May you turn left?
steps: Stop completely at the marked line, or before the crosswalk or intersection if there is no line.
Check both streets. Both are one-way and the turn follows the posted direction. Pennsylvania allows that left turn on red unless signed otherwise.
Yield to pedestrians and other traffic. Turn only when you have a safe opening.
examples.mistake: A ONE WAY sign tells you where traffic moves. It does not cancel the red light or give you priority over someone already crossing.
examples.check: Only the street you want to enter is one-way. Does the same left-turn exception apply?
examples.answer: No. Both streets must be one-way for this exception. Stay stopped until a signal allows the turn.

examples.title: A posted turn restriction settles it
examples.question: In the same Pennsylvania layout you see a NO TURN ON RED sign above the signal. The crosswalk and intersection look empty. Can you turn left after stopping?
steps: No. The posted sign blocks the red-light turn even though both streets are one-way.
Wait until the signal permits the turn.
Check for pedestrians and conflicting traffic before you move.
examples.mistake: An empty intersection is not an exception to a posted turn restriction.
examples.check: The sign is absent, but a cyclist is approaching on the crossing street with the right of way. Can you turn in front of them?
examples.answer: Not if the turn would conflict. The absence of a sign does not remove your duty to yield; wait for a safe gap.

new-jersey-mvc-road-signs-practice.heading: New Jersey: a one-way arrow does not give you a left on red
new-jersey-mvc-road-signs-practice.intro: Use these practice cases to separate the signal, permitted direction and right of way. They cover an ordinary steady circular red light, with no officer, sign or special signal giving different instructions.

examples.title: The intersection looks just like one across the state line
examples.question: You are in the left lane of a one-way street in New Jersey, facing a round red light. The crossing street is one-way to your left and the intersection looks clear. May you turn left after stopping?
steps: No. The one-way layout does not create a left-on-red exception in this New Jersey example.
Stay stopped until the signal permits the turn.
The ordinary exception after a stop applies to a right turn, not this left turn.
examples.mistake: Do not import a rule from Pennsylvania just because the ONE WAY arrows and the street layout look the same.
examples.check: The signal now permits the left turn, but someone is crossing the street you would enter. Does the change mean you can turn through the crosswalk?
examples.answer: No. Wait until you can complete the turn safely without crossing the pedestrian's path.

examples.title: The right turn is available, but the crosswalk is occupied
examples.question: You now intend to turn right on a round red light in New Jersey. There is no turn restriction, but a person is crossing the road you would enter. What should you do?
steps: Come to a full stop before beginning the turn.
Remain stopped for the crossing pedestrian.
Only make the right turn when you have yielded to traffic, can turn safely, and no sign prohibits it.
examples.mistake: A permitted right turn is not a right of way. A stop is necessary; it is not enough when someone is still crossing.
examples.check: The crosswalk clears, but now you notice a NO TURN ON RED sign. Can you make the right turn?
examples.answer: No. Stay stopped until the signal permits the turn. A clear crosswalk does not override a posted restriction.

source.label: New Jersey Driver Manual: Turning Regulations (PDF)

florida-class-e-knowledge-exam-tlsae.heading: Read the words that change a Florida test answer
florida-class-e-knowledge-exam-tlsae.intro: These are original Florida study examples, not official questions. For each one, name the usual rule, then identify the word or condition that changes what you should do.

examples.title: Unless: a posted sign removes the permission
examples.question: You stop at the line for a steady circular red. The intersection is clear, but you see a NO TURN ON RED sign. Can you turn right now?
steps: Start with the red light: stop at the marked line. A right turn can be allowed after stopping and yielding.
Read the exception: unless a sign prohibits it. This sign does. Wait until the signal allows the turn and the way is clear.
examples.mistake: Seeing no traffic does not cancel the sign. Unless tells you which condition blocks the usual permission.
examples.check: Now there is no sign, but a person is using the crosswalk. Can you turn after stopping?
examples.answer: Not yet. The sign exception no longer applies, but you still have to yield. Turn only when you can do so safely and legally.

source.label: Florida Statutes 316.075(1)(c): turning at a steady red

examples.title: Not less than: the number is a minimum
examples.question: You are behind a cyclist in your travel lane. There would be three feet of clearance, but you cannot see far enough around a bend to pass safely. Should you pass now?
steps: Not less than three feet means three feet or more, not three feet or less.
That distance is a minimum. If you cannot make the pass safely, stay a safe distance behind the cyclist.
examples.mistake: Meeting the distance alone is not permission to pass. The move itself must be safe.
examples.check: The road straightens, but you could leave only two and a half feet. What do you do?
examples.answer: Stay back. Better visibility does not remove the minimum clearance.

source.label: Florida Statutes 316.083(2): passing a cyclist in the same lane

examples.title: Until: look for the event that ends the wait
examples.question: You are stopped behind a school bus. A child reaches the sidewalk, but the bus still displays its stop signal. Can you pass?
steps: Until tells you what ends the restriction. For a driver behind the bus, wait until its stop signal is withdrawn.
Keep looking for children and other traffic before moving. One child reaching the sidewalk does not end the stop.
examples.mistake: The first thing you can see happening is not necessarily the event the rule names.
examples.check: Instead, you approach in the opposite direction on a divided road, with a raised median between you and the bus. Does Florida require you to stop for that bus?
examples.answer: No, not under the school-bus rule in this situation. Florida's exception applies to opposing traffic separated by a raised median, a physical barrier, or at least five feet of unpaved space. It does not excuse a driver following the bus.

source.label: Florida Statutes 316.172: stopping for a school bus

sat-device-troubleshooting-guide.heading: Three Bluebook device problems to solve before the SAT
sat-device-troubleshooting-guide.intro: These examples are fictional. Check the requirements for your actual device and follow your school's instructions for SAT School Day.

examples.title: Your Windows 10 laptop is not ready, and the SAT is in 18 days
examples.question: You can study on your Windows 10 laptop, but it does not meet the current Windows requirement for Bluebook. Can you count on a College Board loaner for this weekend date?
steps: Do not plan to test on Windows 10. Check an alternative device now: for example, ask your school or someone you know about a supported device you can prepare before test day.
The standard College Board loaner deadline for this date has already passed. If you cannot arrange an approved device, check College Board's help or a later date before assuming you can test.
examples.mistake: Opening a prep website does not show that the device can run the test. The lending deadline is separate from the registration and exam-setup windows.
examples.check: What changes if the test is 36 days away and you still have no approved device?
examples.answer: You have time to follow the SAT Weekend lending steps: register, complete the request in My SAT at least 30 days before testing, and arrange the required non-family adult verification. A request still does not guarantee approval.

examples.title: Your school-managed Chromebook fails Verified Mode
examples.question: Your school Chromebook opens Bluebook, but Test Your Device shows Verified Mode is not enabled. What should you do?
steps: Tell your school's technology team what Bluebook reported. The school manages installation and Verified Mode; a student cannot prepare the Chromebook by installing the app independently.
After the school fixes it, run Test Your Device again. If it cannot be fixed in time, ask the school about an approved replacement and how to prepare it.
examples.mistake: Being school-managed and opening the app are not enough. Do not assume a personal Chromebook is an acceptable backup.
examples.check: What if this is SAT School Day rather than SAT Weekend?
examples.answer: Follow your school's device and sign-in instructions. The College Board request process for a weekend loaner does not replace the school's plan.

examples.title: You need a replacement after generating your admission ticket
examples.question: You completed SAT Weekend exam setup on a borrowed Mac. Two days before testing, it breaks. A supported iPad is available. Is your earlier ticket enough to prepare the iPad?
steps: Check the replacement against current Bluebook requirements. Open the app and run Test Your Device on the iPad.
Sign in and complete exam setup on that replacement. Check that you have your current admission ticket for test day. Do not assume the old device's setup carried over.
examples.mistake: A ticket is not proof that the replacement device is ready. Setup must be completed on the device you use.
examples.check: What if the device fails after timed testing has started?
examples.answer: Tell your proctor immediately. Let staff direct any device swap; do not start another test or independently switch devices.

ap-scores-delayed-missing-2026.heading: Three missing-score cases
ap-scores-delayed-missing-2026.intro: Fictional examples using the 2026 release. Start by checking your own College Board score report, then verify any college requirement directly.

examples.title: One result is missing from your account
examples.question: It is November 2026. You see AP English Language in your original College Board account, but AP Chemistry from a late-testing date is still absent. What would you do first?
steps: Write down the subject, late-testing date and school. Note that another 2026 score appears in the same account.
The August 15 support checkpoint has passed. Contact AP Services for Students with those facts. Ask whether it can locate the Chemistry exam record.
examples.mistake: Late testing might explain an initial delay, but it does not identify what is holding this specific score now.
examples.check: What if you cannot sign in to the account you used for AP?
examples.answer: Use College Board's account recovery help first. Creating another account can complicate matching.

examples.title: Your college has not posted a visible score
examples.question: Your AP Biology score appears in College Board. Your order history shows the report was made available to the correct college, but its student portal has not posted the credit. Would another report address the problem?
steps: Check that the reporting recipient matches the college you attend and that the report includes the Biology result.
Ask the college's registrar or admissions office whether it matched the report and when its placement or credit decision is due.
examples.mistake: Available to the recipient does not mean processed by the college. Paying for another report would not confirm that processing occurred.
examples.check: What if your order history shows a different college?
examples.answer: Confirm the correct recipient and the required report with your college. A report sent to one college is not delivery to another.

examples.title: Placement is due while a score is still pending
examples.question: Your college already received a 2026 AP report with the available results, but you need the missing Calculus result for placement. Registration opens next week. Can you count on an automatic update in time?
steps: Check that the college was designated to receive your scores from that exam year. College Board can send a delayed score automatically once it becomes available.
Contact AP Services about the absent 2026 result and ask the college how to register while placement is pending. Keep the two conversations separate.
examples.mistake: Automatic sending has no guaranteed date for the score to appear or the college to apply it. Ordering another report does not create the absent score.
examples.check: What if the college confirms it accepts an alternative placement test?
examples.answer: Check its deadline and how the result would affect registration. Follow the confirmed option while you resolve the AP record with AP Services.

sat-score-release-guide.heading: Three application deadlines, three different decisions
sat-score-release-guide.intro: College Board lists December 18, 2026 as the student release date for the December 5 SAT Weekend. The college rules and deadlines below are fictional. Use your own college's written policy and verify when your score actually appears.

examples.title: A college accepts self-reporting
examples.question: Your college accepts the December SAT and lets you enter scores in its application portal through December 20. Your score appears December 18. Do you need to order an official score report to meet this deadline?
steps: Use the college's self-reporting field and confirm the portal shows the score was submitted before its cutoff.
Save the submission confirmation. Check when the college requires an official report, if it does; it might be needed later rather than with the application.
examples.mistake: Avoid paying for delivery just because the application deadline is close. A self-reporting deadline is not the same as an official receipt deadline.
examples.check: What if the college does not accept self-reported scores?
examples.answer: Follow the college's official receipt rule. Entering your score in a text box is not a substitute for a required official report.

examples.title: A college must receive the official report
examples.question: Your score appears Friday, December 18. The college accepts the December test but requires the official report by Monday, December 21. Would ordering on Friday give you a reliable delivery plan?
steps: Standard delivery is typically sent 5 to 10 business days after you order; the weekend does not leave that much time.

Rush is available only after release and is sent in 1 to 4 business days, excluding weekends and holidays. Even the fastest end of that range leaves no time to spare. The college may need more time to match the report to your application.
Before paying, ask whether the college can use an earlier score, accept a pending score, or honor a separate materials deadline. If it cannot, plan using the written requirement.
examples.mistake: An order receipt is not a delivery confirmation, and a report marked sent is not necessarily posted to your application.
examples.check: What if the portal shows a different materials deadline from the application deadline?
examples.answer: Verify which cutoff applies to official scores, which test dates the college accepts, and what the deadline means: ordered, received, or matched. Use the college's confirmed rule.

examples.title: The deadline comes before the scheduled release
examples.question: Your college needs scores by December 15. Your new December SAT score is scheduled for December 18, and you already have a score from an earlier test. Can a rush order make the December score usable by December 15?
steps: No. Rush applies to released scores only. The new score is not scheduled to be available by the college's deadline.
Check whether the earlier sitting is accepted and how to report it. Ask about a later materials cutoff only if the college's policy leaves that unclear.
examples.mistake: An SAT date before the application deadline is not enough. Compare the accepted test date and the score deadline separately.
examples.check: What if the college is test optional for your program?
examples.answer: Check whether the program, scholarship or applicant category has an exception. If the college confirms you can apply without a score, that is a separate option from ordering an older report.

sat-math-score-guide.heading: Work an error through to a new problem
sat-math-score-guide.intro: Original teaching examples, not College Board questions or a score estimate. Try each problem before opening the reasoning, then test the same skill with the changed problem.

examples.title: Find the first wrong step
examples.question: A student changes 4(2x - 3) = 20 into 8x - 3 = 20 and obtains x = 23/8. Identify the first error, then solve and check the original equation.
steps: The factor 4 multiplies both terms inside the parentheses: 8x - 12 = 20, not 8x - 3 = 20.
Add 12 to both sides: 8x = 32. Divide by 8: x = 4.
Substitute into the original equation: 4(2 times 4 - 3) = 4 times 5 = 20. The answer satisfies the original, not just a later line.
examples.mistake: Review label: distribution. If you reached 23/8, the issue was the first expansion, not division at the end. On your next practice problem, write the expanded line explicitly.
examples.check: Changed problem: solve 3(2x - 5) = 21. Write the expanded line and one substitution check before opening the answer.
examples.answer: 6x - 15 = 21; 6x = 36; x = 6. Check: 3(2 times 6 - 5) = 3 times 7 = 21. Both terms were multiplied by 3.

examples.title: Separate a starting amount from a rate
examples.question: A bicycle rental costs a fixed $8 plus $3 per hour. A student writes C = 8h + 3. What is wrong with the model, and what should a two-hour rental cost?
steps: Let h be rental time in hours and C be cost in dollars. Each additional hour adds $3, so the variable part is 3h.
The fixed $8 does not depend on hours. Add it once: C = 3h + 8.
For two hours, C = 3(2) + 8 = $14. The student's model gives $19 because it incorrectly makes $8 the hourly rate.
Check the structure: when h increases by 1, the correct model increases C by $3. The units of 3h are dollars per hour times hours, which is dollars.
examples.mistake: Review label: interpreting a linear model. A calculator can evaluate either model, but cannot decide which quantity is the rate. Label the rate and fixed amount before calculating.
examples.check: Changed problem: another rental uses C = 5h + 12. Interpret 12, then calculate the total for three hours and the additional cost of one more hour.
examples.answer: 12 is the fixed starting cost, in dollars. Three hours cost 5(3) + 12 = $27. One additional hour adds $5, not another $12.

sat-reading-writing-score-guide.heading: Test the reason behind an answer
sat-reading-writing-score-guide.intro: Original teaching examples, not College Board questions or a score estimate. Choose an answer before opening the reasoning. The changed question checks whether the reason transfers beyond a memorized answer.

examples.title: Choose the relationship, not a familiar phrase
examples.question: A library predicted that longer evening hours would increase attendance. It stayed open two hours later for a month. ___, its evening attendance remained unchanged. Which transition fits: A. Consequently; B. However; C. For example; D. Similarly?
steps: Compare the prediction with the outcome. The library expected an increase, but attendance stayed the same. The relationship is contrast.
B, However, marks that contrast. A, Consequently, would emphasize an effect rather than the failure of the stated prediction.
C, For example, would require a general statement that this outcome illustrates. D, Similarly, would require a comparable result already described. Neither relationship is supplied.
examples.mistake: Review label: transitions. All four choices can begin a sentence grammatically. Grammar alone cannot choose between them; first state the relationship between the ideas in your own words.
examples.check: Changed question: a library wanted to make its services easier to access. ___, it extended evening hours and added a weekend book-return point. Which choice fits: For example, However, or Nevertheless? Explain what the second sentence does.
examples.answer: For example. Extending hours and adding a return point illustrate the general aim of easier access. However and Nevertheless would signal an opposition that this text does not establish.

examples.title: Match a conclusion to the evidence's scope
examples.question: In one class, the average practice score rose from 61 to 65 after a new study routine was introduced. There was no comparison class. Which conclusion is supported: A. Every student improved; B. The routine caused the increase; C. This class's average was four points higher afterward; D. The routine works better for all students?
steps: The two reported averages establish a four-point increase for this class. C stays within those observations.
A is too broad: an average does not show each student's change. For example, scores of 50 and 72 average 61; scores of 48 and 82 average 65 even though one score fell.

B adds causation that a before-and-after observation without a comparison does not establish. D extends one class to all students and adds a comparison with other methods. Neither claim is given by the evidence.
examples.mistake: Review label: evidence and inference. A choice may repeat the right topic while adding every, caused, or all. Check the population, comparison and strength of the claim against the actual observations.
examples.check: Changed question: both classes improved, but the report gives only their averages and no individual results. Can you conclude that every student in either class improved? What narrower statement could you make?
examples.answer: No. You can report that each class's average increased, but not that every individual's score rose. The numerical counterexample above shows why those are different claims.
